A libretto is the complete written text of an opera or a similar large-scale musical vocal work. It contains all the words that are sung — and sometimes spoken — by the performers on stage.

Think of it this way: a film has a screenplay. A play has a script. An opera has a libretto. It plays the same role — it's the literary foundation of the entire work.
What exactly is in a libretto?

A libretto is a full document that typically includes:

  • All the sung words — every line that a singer performs, whether it's a solo aria (a song sung by one person), a duet, or a full chorus number.
  • Recitative — this is a style halfway between singing and speaking, used to move the story forward between the big musical moments. The words for this are in the libretto too.
  • Spoken dialogue — in some musical works, characters speak rather than sing certain lines. Those are included as well.
  • Stage directions — brief instructions like "she enters from the left" or "he collapses to the floor," which guide the performers and directors.

So a libretto is not just lyrics. It's the entire verbal blueprint of the performance.

The person who writes a libretto is called a librettist. This is a separate craft from composing music, and historically, the librettist was considered a creative collaborator of equal importance to the composer.

Sometimes, however, the composer and librettist are the same person. The famous German composer Richard Wagner wrote all his own libretti. But more commonly, they are two different people working together — the librettist shapes the story and the language, and the composer then sets those words to music.
What kinds of works have a libretto?

The word "libretto" is mainly used for these types of works:

  • Opera — the most common. An opera is a full dramatic story performed entirely (or almost entirely) through singing, with an orchestra. Every major opera — La Traviata, The Magic Flute, Carmen — has a libretto.
  • Oratorio — a large choral work, usually on a religious or epic subject, performed without costumes or staging. Handel's Messiah is a famous example. It has a libretto even though there's no acting.
  • Operetta — a lighter, shorter, often comic form of opera (like the works of Gilbert & Sullivan). Also has a libretto.
  • Musical theatre — this is a grey area. The spoken text in a musical is usually called the book, and the sung words are called lyrics. But sometimes the full text is informally referred to as a libretto, especially in academic or formal contexts.

The key point: "libretto" belongs to the world of classical and semi-classical musical performance, not everyday pop music. You wouldn't call a Taylor Swift song's words a "libretto" — those are simply lyrics.
How does the libretto relate to the music?

The libretto and the music are two halves of the same work, but they exist separately. The score (the written-out musical notation) tells the performers what notes to play and sing. The libretto tells them what words those notes carry.

When a composer receives a libretto, they study it carefully. They feel the rhythm of the language, the emotion of each scene, the dramatic tension building across acts. Then they write music that matches and amplifies all of that. A great libretto gives the composer dramatic peaks to build toward, intimate moments to make tender, and comic lines to make funny — all through language that sounds beautiful when sung.

This is why the libretto matters so much: bad words make bad opera, no matter how brilliant the music.
How the libretto was historically used by audiences

In the era before subtitles and surtitles (the projected text you see above the stage in modern opera houses), audiences — especially those who didn't speak Italian, German, or French — would buy a small printed booklet of the libretto before the performance. They could read along during the show to understand what was happening.

This booklet form is actually baked into the word itself — a libretto is literally a "little book,".

It helps to know how "libretto" sits among related terms:

  • Score — the complete musical notation of the whole work (notes, rhythms, instrumentation). The score contains the libretto within it, but also everything else.
  • Lyrics — the words of a song. A casual, everyday word. "Libretto" is the formal term for the full text of an extended classical vocal work.
  • Script / Screenplay — the text of a play or film. A libretto is the equivalent for opera and oratorio.
  • Book (in musicals) — the spoken dialogue portion of a musical. Sometimes "libretto" covers both the book and the lyrics together in formal usage.

The plural of libretto is either libretti (the Italian form, preferred in classical music circles) or librettos (the fully anglicized version, also perfectly acceptable in everyday use). Both are correct.
A concrete example to lock it in

Take Mozart's opera The Marriage of Figaro. A man named Lorenzo Da Ponte sat down and wrote the full story — all the characters, all the scenes, all the words to be sung and spoken. That text is the libretto. Mozart then took that libretto and composed the music for every line of it. When you watch the opera performed on stage, the singers are performing both the libretto (Da Ponte's words) and the score (Mozart's music) simultaneously. Neither exists properly without the other.

A libretto is the complete written text — the words — of an opera, oratorio, or similar large-scale musical work. It is to a musical performance what a script is to a play. Written by a librettist, it contains all sung lines, spoken dialogue, and stage directions. The composer then takes the libretto and writes music to bring those words to life. Without the libretto, there is no opera — just music with nowhere to go.
